original_value:
Defense mechanisms against network-level attacks are commonly based on the use of cryptographic techniques, such as lengthy message authentication codes (MAC) that provide data integrity guarantees. However, such mechanisms require significant resources (both computational and network bandwidth), which prevents their continuous use in resource-constrained cyber-physical systems (CPS). Recently, it was shown how physical properties of controlled systems can be exploited to relax these stringent requirements for systems where sensor measurements and actuator commands are transmitted over a potentially compromised network; specifically, that merely intermittent use of data authentication (i.e., at occasional time points during system execution), can still provide strong Quality-of-Control (QoC) guarantees even in the presence of false-data injection attacks, such as
            Man-in-the-Middle
            (MitM) attacks. Consequently, in this work, we focus on integrating security into existing resource-constrained CPS, in order to protect against MitM attacks on a system where a set of control tasks communicates over a real-time network with system sensors and actuators. We introduce a design-time methodology that incorporates requirements for QoC in the presence of attacks into end-to-end timing constraints for real-time control transactions, which include data acquisition and authentication, real-time network messages, and control tasks. This allows us to formulate a mixed integer linear programming-based method for direct synthesis of schedulable tasks and message parameters (i.e., deadlines and offsets) that do not violate timing requirements for the already deployed controllers, while adding a sufficient level of protection against network-based attacks; specifically, the synthesis method also provides suitable intermittent authentication policies that ensure the desired QoC levels under attack. To additionally reduce the security-related bandwidth overhead, we propose the use of cumulative message authentication at time instances when the integrity of messages from subsets of sensors should be ensured. Furthermore, we introduce a method for the opportunistic use of the remaining resources to further improve the overall QoC guarantees while ensuring system (i.e., task and message) schedulability. Finally, we demonstrate applicability and scalability of our methodology on synthetic automotive systems as well as a real-world automotive case-study.

result.paraphrase: This work integrates security into resource-constrained cyber-physical systems to defend against Man-in-the-Middle attacks on a setup where control tasks communicate with sensors and actuators over a real-time network. Building on recent results showing that physical properties of controlled systems can enable intermittent data authentication while still preserving strong Quality-of-Control guarantees under false-data injection attacks, we present a design-time method that embeds attack-aware QoC requirements into end-to-end timing constraints for real-time control transactions. These transactions cover data acquisition and authentication, real-time network messages, and control tasks. Using this framework, we formulate a mixed-integer linear programming approach that directly synthesizes schedulable tasks and message parameters, including deadlines and offsets, without breaking the timing requirements of already deployed controllers, while still providing sufficient protection against network-based attacks. The synthesis also yields intermittent authentication policies that achieve the target QoC under attack. To further reduce security-related bandwidth overhead, we propose cumulative message authentication at times when integrity must be guaranteed for messages from sensor subsets. We also introduce a way to opportunistically use remaining resources to improve overall QoC guarantees while preserving task and message schedulability. Finally, we show the method’s applicability and scalability on synthetic automotive systems and a real-world automotive case study.
